key_terms.meaning: Concentration of Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions in water, expressed as mg CaCO₃ per L.
Ca hardness plus Mg hardness after converting both to equivalent CaCO₃.
Hardness caused by bicarbonates of Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺; removed by boiling.
Hardness caused by chlorides, sulfates or nitrates of Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺; not removed by boiling.
Mass of dissolved solids per litre of water, usually mg/L.
Cloudiness from suspended particles, measured in NTU.
Oxygen used by microbes to oxidise organic matter in water, usually mg/L over 5 days.
Hard adherent deposit such as CaCO₃ or Mg(OH)₂ formed on hot boiler surfaces.
Loose suspended precipitate in boiler water that settles in low-flow zones.
Intercrystalline cracking of boiler steel caused by concentrated NaOH at stressed seams.
Carryover of boiler water droplets with steam.
Precipitation softening using Ca(OH)₂ and Na₂CO₃ to convert soluble hardness into CaCO₃ and Mg(OH)₂.
Ion-exchange softening in which Na⁺ on a zeolite or resin is exchanged for Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺.
Addition of a chemical such as alum to neutralise colloid charge and start particle clumping.
Gentle stirring that makes small coagulated particles collide and grow into settleable flocs.
Disinfection by chlorine, hypochlorous acid or hypochlorite.
Chlorine species left in treated water to prevent regrowth of microbes in the distribution system.
Pressure-driven membrane process that passes water while rejecting dissolved ions when applied pressure exceeds osmotic pressure.
Pressure that must be applied to a solution to stop net solvent flow through a semipermeable membrane.
Desalination using a DC electric field to move ions through alternating cation- and anion-selective membranes.

takeaways: Water quality is judged by measured parameters compared with drinking-water or feed-water standards.
Hardness is the sum of Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ expressed as CaCO₃ equivalent, not the separate ion concentrations.
Carbonate hardness is removed by boiling; non-carbonate hardness needs chemical or ion-exchange softening.
Every boiler trouble has a source impurity: hardness makes scale, oxygen and CO₂ cause corrosion, high NaOH can cause caustic embrittlement.
External softening removes hardness before the boiler; internal conditioning controls the small amount left inside.
A municipal plant follows a fixed train: screening, coagulation and flocculation, sedimentation, filtration and disinfection.
Chlorination must leave a residual to protect water in the pipe network after the plant.
RO uses pressure above osmotic pressure to push water through a membrane; electrodialysis uses a DC field to pull ions through selective membranes.
bank_note: Long answers usually stress a labelled flow diagram, the reaction or formula at each step, and a reasoned choice between treatment options.

bank.q: Define hardness of water. Distinguish carbonate hardness from non-carbonate hardness, and write the expression for total hardness as CaCO₃.
outline: Hardness is Ca²⁺ plus Mg²⁺ expressed as CaCO₃
Carbonate hardness comes from bicarbonates and is removed by boiling
Non-carbonate hardness comes from chlorides and sulfates and is not removed by boiling
Total hardness = Ca hardness + Mg hardness as CaCO₃
Report in mg/L as CaCO₃

bank.q: List the common water quality parameters used for drinking water and boiler feed water. State what each parameter measures.
outline: pH
Turbidity
TDS
Hardness
Alkalinity
Dissolved oxygen
BOD and COD
Silica, chloride, iron and residual chlorine
Boiler feed limits are stricter for hardness, oxygen and silica

bank.q: Explain scale and sludge formation in boilers. Give the cause, effect and one control measure for each.
outline: Scale from CaCO₃, Mg(OH)₂ and CaSO₄ on hot surfaces
Scale lowers heat transfer and can overheat metal
Control scale by softening and blowdown
Sludge is a loose precipitate that can settle and choke
Control sludge by blowdown and phosphate treatment

bank.q: Describe the sequence of steps in a municipal water treatment plant and state the impurity removed at each step.
outline: Screening removes large solids
Coagulation and flocculation remove colloidal turbidity
Sedimentation removes flocs
Filtration removes fine particles
Disinfection kills pathogens
Residual chlorine protects the distribution system

bank.q: A water sample contains Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺. Explain how you would calculate total hardness as CaCO₃ from their concentrations. Include the conversion factors and units.
outline: Convert mg Ca²⁺/L to mg CaCO₃/L using 100/40
Convert mg Mg²⁺/L to mg CaCO₃/L using 100/24.3
Total hardness = Ca hardness + Mg hardness
Report as mg/L as CaCO₃
Show a sample calculation
Mention EDTA titration for measurement

bank.q: Compare lime-soda softening with zeolite softening. Write the main reactions and state one advantage and one limitation of each.
outline: Lime-soda uses Ca(OH)₂ and Na₂CO₃
Lime removes temporary hardness and Mg
Soda removes non-carbonate Ca
Lime-soda produces sludge
Zeolite exchanges Na⁺ for Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺
Zeolite needs NaCl regeneration and is not for turbid water

bank.q: Explain breakpoint chlorination with a simple graph of residual chlorine against chlorine dose. Why is breakpoint chlorination used in municipal supply?
outline: Chlorine demand from reducing and organic matter
Combined chlorine forms first
Breakpoint occurs at minimum residual
Free residual appears after breakpoint
Ensures disinfection and leaves residual
Avoids taste and odour from excess combined chlorine

bank.q: Describe reverse osmosis with a labelled diagram. Explain why the applied pressure must exceed the osmotic pressure and name the pretreatment needed for a hard feed water.
outline: Semipermeable membrane
Applied pressure greater than osmotic pressure
Water permeates and ions are rejected
Concentrate stream and recovery
Pretreatment removes hardness, turbidity and chlorine
Scaling control and energy cost

bank.q: Draw an electrodialysis stack and explain how cation- and anion-selective membranes separate ions into dilute and concentrate streams.
outline: DC electrodes
Alternating cation and anion membranes
Cations move toward cathode and anions toward anode
Salt concentration alternates in compartments
Dilute and concentrate streams leave the stack
Polarity reversal helps control fouling

bank.q: A boiler shows scale on tubes, corrosion pits and occasional caustic cracking. Relate each trouble to a likely feed-water impurity and propose a control measure.
outline: Scale from Ca and Mg hardness; soften feed and control blowdown
Corrosion pits from dissolved O₂ and CO₂; deaerate and use oxygen scavenger
Caustic cracking from high NaOH at stressed seams; control alkalinity and use phosphate or coordinated pH
Testing and monitoring of feed and boiler water

bank.q: Compare external and internal treatment of boiler feed water. For a plant using very hard water, recommend a treatment train and justify each unit.
outline: External treatment: lime-soda, zeolite or demineralisation before boiler
Internal treatment: phosphate, hydrazine, amines and blowdown
Hard water needs external softening first
Deaeration follows softening
Internal conditioning handles residual hardness and oxygen
Consider economics and steam purity

bank.q: A city source is turbid and contaminated with sewage. Evaluate the treatment train needed to produce safe drinking water and explain where chlorination should be applied.
outline: Coagulation and flocculation for turbidity
Sedimentation and filtration
Disinfection after filtration
Chlorine dose and contact time
Residual chlorine in distribution
Monitor pH and turbidity and avoid excess trihalomethane

bank.q: A textile plant has hard, brackish well water. Compare softening followed by reverse osmosis with electrodialysis, and recommend one route with reasons.
outline: Hardness causes scaling; soften before membrane processes
RO removes ions and organics
ED removes ions only and needs pretreatment for turbidity and hardness
Compare energy, recovery, fouling and brine disposal
Recommend RO for high TDS with organic load
Recommend ED for brackish water with low organics
Justify with cost and product quality

glossary.def: The set of physical, chemical and biological measurements used to judge whether water is fit for a stated use.
The concentration of Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ in water, expressed as mg CaCO₃ per litre.
The mass of CaCO₃ that would give the same number of equivalents as the ion being reported.
The total mass of dissolved solids in a known volume of water, usually reported as mg/L.
The cloudiness of water caused by suspended particles, measured in nephelometric turbidity units.
The oxygen consumed by microorganisms while oxidising organic matter in water, usually over five days and reported as mg/L.
The oxygen equivalent of organic matter oxidised by a strong chemical oxidant, reported as mg/L.
The concentration of dissolved oxygen gas in water, usually mg/L.
The capacity of water to neutralise acid, mainly from bicarbonate, carbonate and hydroxide ions, reported as mg/L as CaCO₃.
A hard deposit such as CaCO₃ or Mg(OH)₂ that forms on hot boiler surfaces.
A loose precipitate suspended in boiler water that can settle in low-flow regions.
Cracking of boiler steel along grain boundaries caused by concentrated NaOH at stressed seams.
The carryover of droplets of boiler water into steam.
Attack on boiler metal by dissolved oxygen, carbon dioxide or acid, producing pits and thinning.
Removal of Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ from water to reduce hardness.
Precipitation softening with Ca(OH)₂ and Na₂CO₃, which convert soluble hardness ions into CaCO₃ and Mg(OH)₂.
A natural or synthetic ion-exchange material that swaps Na⁺ for Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ in water softening.
Reversible exchange of ions between a solid resin and a solution.
Restoring an exhausted ion-exchange resin by washing it with a concentrated solution such as NaCl.
Destabilisation of colloidal particles by a chemical coagulant so that they can stick together.
Gentle mixing that brings destabilised particles into contact so they grow into larger flocs.
Disinfection of water with chlorine gas, hypochlorite or hypochlorous acid.
The chlorine species left after treatment that protect the distribution system against microbial regrowth.
A pressure-driven membrane process that passes water while rejecting most dissolved ions when the applied pressure exceeds osmotic pressure.
The pressure that must be applied to a solution to stop net flow of solvent through a semipermeable membrane.
A desalination process in which a DC electric field moves ions through ion-selective membranes into concentrate streams.
